title: Night of the Grizzlies
summary: Josh and Chuck tell the story of the Night of the Grizzlies, August 12-13, 1967, when two nineteen-year-old women, Julie Helgeson and Michelle Coons, were killed by two different grizzly bears in Glacier National Park on the same night. They cover grizzly biology and the decline of grizzlies under westward expansion, the unsafe park practices of the era (feeding bears for tourist entertainment, garbage dumps, the Granite Park Chalet feeding area), a blow-by-blow account of both attacks, the manhunt and killing of bears, the Craighead brothers' conservation push, later policy changes such as bear-proof garbage and food storage, grizzly recovery and Endangered Species Act listing, and bear attack odds. The episode ends with a listener mail about Hammond electric clocks and a sign-off.

segments.title: Vinyl LP promo
segments.summary: Hosts promote the Stuff You Should Know vinyl podcast LP, available from Born Losers Records.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode title and tease the story of two women killed by grizzly bears in one night.

segments.title: Overview and grizzly bear biology
segments.summary: Overview of the August 1967 deaths in Glacier National Park, which were rare in the park's history. Discussion of grizzlies as a subspecies of brown bear, their size and naming, and their historic decline from expansion into the West.

segments.title: Bears and park tourism
segments.summary: Discussion of why bears were in conflict with people, including the bears' habituation to human food and park practices that let tourists approach them.

segments.title: Causes of bear aggression in 1967
segments.summary: Explains why bear encounters increased, including the highway-driven tourist surge and the 1967 fires. Describes an emaciated female bear that had been aggressive and brazen. Hosts note that park administrators bore responsibility for the situation.

segments.title: Julie Helgeson and Michelle Coons set out
segments.summary: Introduces Julie Helgeson and Michelle Coons, both nineteen and working summer jobs at Glacier. They separately set out on hikes on August 12, 1967. Helgeson and Roy Ducott camped near Granite Park Chalet, which was a site of purposeful bear feeding.

segments.title: Helgeson attack and delayed search
segments.summary: Describes the bear attack on Roy Ducott and Julie Helgeson just after midnight, Ducott's rescue by helicopter, and the roughly two-hour wait before the search for Helgeson. She was found and taken to the chalet, where she died of blood loss and shock.

segments.title: Coons group camping and the night bear attacks
segments.summary: Describes the group camping at Trout Lake, a bear that visited at 8 pm and at 3 am and took food, and the final attack around 4:30 am that ended with Michelle Coons being dragged off. Other campers escaped, and a sixteen-year-old climbed a tree.

segments.title: Discovery of Coons body and ranger response
segments.summary: Ranger Bert Gildart is woken and informed of the Trout Lake attack. Ranger Leonard Landa finds Michelle Coons' partially eaten body.

segments.title: Bear hunt and killing of bears
segments.summary: Park officials form a search party to find and shoot the bears involved. Rangers kill a bear that approaches them, and examination finds glass in its molars and human hair in its stomach. Another bear and cubs are shot at the chalet garbage pit.

segments.title: Media coverage and Sports Illustrated story
segments.summary: Discusses media speculation about causes, such as lightning and menstrual blood, and notes Jack Olsen's Sports Illustrated article, later a book, as the standard account.

segments.title: Eradication push and Craighead brothers
segments.summary: Gardner Dyment proposed eliminating grizzlies. The Craighead brothers, Frank and John, countered with research and common-sense measures that turned public opinion toward conservation.

segments.title: Park policy changes and grizzly recovery
segments.summary: Describes safety measures such as separating people from bear areas and tracking bears, and closing Yellowstone's garbage dumps too abruptly. Cites a 1972 camper death, about 189 bears killed from 1968 to 1973, and the 1975 Endangered Species Act listing. Recovery brings the population to nearly two thousand, and hunting is discussed.

segments.title: Bear safety practices and attack odds
segments.summary: Covers bear-proof garbage cans, hanging food, and National Park Service odds of injury by bear. Hosts discuss the importance of responsible behavior in bear country.

segments.title: Listener mail: Hammond electric clock
segments.summary: Tim and Sarah write in about their Hammond electric clock, which had low-voltage bulbs and requires a restart after a power outage.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and sign off, with a note about the iHeartRadio production.
